texts.text: Research on how second-language writers revise after written corrective feedback (WCF) converges on a distinction between immediate text improvement and durable accuracy gains, though the evidence base is uneven.
This methodological profile matters for interpreting the revision literature: descriptive accounts of uptake predominate over designs capable of isolating feedback type.
Direct corrections appear to support longer-term accuracy where metalinguistic codes do not.
Evidence on automated feedback remains largely corpus- or case-based, with limited classroom uptake data.

texts.text: Direct written corrective feedback (WCF), which supplies the correct form, and indirect WCF, which locates or codes errors without supplying it, differ in the interpretive demands they place on L2 writers.
Experimental classroom evidence indicates that both forms can support accuracy gains during revision, though their durability differs.
Whether these strands converge on a single account of direct versus indirect WCF remains unresolved.

### 2.2 Revision Behaviour Under Automated Feedback
Peer-mediated revision involving Grammarly alongside self-reflection produced rubric gains between drafts (Li & Hebert, 2023), though a causal role for self-reflection was not established.
### 2.3 Teacher and Learner Engagement
### 2.4 Synthesis and Research Gaps

Taken together, the library indicates that AWCF can match or exceed established tools on precision and on some error categories while remaining weaker on others, and that engagement with automated feedback varies widely across learners and teachers.

Three gaps follow: no library study compares AWCF with teacher feedback on accuracy in a controlled design; teacher–tool interaction has been examined only through one-time hypothetical scenarios (Koltovskaia, 2022); and prompt-design effects on learner revision outcomes remain untested.
These gaps motivate the present study's comparison of feedback conditions.

texts.text: Research on written corrective feedback (WCF) in second-language (L2) writing has shifted from asking whether feedback works to asking how learners engage with it and how teacher, peer, and automated sources compare [NEEDS CITATION].
Evidence on the accuracy effects of peer feedback is limited and largely indirect [NEEDS CITATION].
Uptake of peer comments is uneven.
Comparative evidence on teacher versus automated feedback is sparse.

Across these sources, peer WCF is associated with revision improvements and generally positive usefulness ratings, yet the evidence base is dominated by small, qualitative, single-context designs [NEEDS CITATION].

Three gaps follow: no direct experimental comparison of peer, teacher, and automated WCF on accuracy; limited evidence on the conditions governing uptake; and an affective dimension that remains unexamined [NEEDS CITATION].
